CHAPTER 1 OF 3 · SCALP AND OCCIPITAL BLOCKS

Anatomy: the nerves of the scalp

The scalp has five layers (SCALP): skin, connective tissue (carrying the vessels and nerves), aponeurosis, loose areolar tissue and pericranium. The nerves run in the connective tissue layer, so they can all be reached with a shallow injection once they have come through the deep fascia.

text.ch-scalp:
CHAPTER 2 OF 3 · SCALP · LANDMARK

Scalp block

Small volumes of local anaesthetic at the six or seven nerves that supply the scalp, where each one becomes superficial: three branches of the trigeminal nerve in front and two (or three) branches of C2–C3 behind. An anatomical block, not a ring of infiltration.

USE IT FOR

Awake craniotomy
Head pins (Mayfield) and skin incision under general anaesthesia: blunts the blood pressure surge
Analgesia after craniotomy
Scalp lacerations and lesions
POSITION
Supine, head turned or in pins; all sites reachable
PROBE
None: landmarks
NEEDLE
25–27G, 25–40 mm
DOSE
About 2–5 ml at each site; 20–30 ml in total
COVERS
The whole scalp, one side per set of injections

The seven injection sites (right side)

Supratrochlear (V1): above the medial end of the eyebrow, at the bridge of the nose.
Supraorbital (V1): at the supraorbital notch, on the upper orbital rim in line with the pupil.
Zygomaticotemporal (V2): from the lateral orbital rim back along the top of the zygomatic arch, deep and superficial to temporalis fascia.
Auriculotemporal (V3): 1–1.5 cm in front of the tragus, behind the superficial temporal artery.
Great auricular (C2–C3, optional): about 1.5 cm behind the ear at the level of the tragus.
Lesser occipital (C2): a third of the way along the superior nuchal line from the mastoid to the occipital protuberance; infiltrate up behind the ear.
Greater occipital (C2): two-thirds of the way from the mastoid to the occipital protuberance, just medial to the occipital artery.

Schematic, not to scale.

Position

Supine, before the head is fixed in pins, or with the head turned to reach the back. Block both sides for a bifrontal or midline incision.

Equipment
Fine needle (25–27G), long enough to fan along the superior nuchal line
Local anaesthetic with adrenaline, for example lidocaine 0.75% with bupivacaine 0.25% and adrenaline 1:200 000.
Monitoring: injections around the face and occiput are close to vessels
Landmarks and injections
Supraorbital: feel the supraorbital notch and inject just above it, perpendicular to the eyebrow.
Supratrochlear: just medial to the supraorbital injection, at the bridge of the nose.
Zygomaticotemporal: infiltrate from the lateral orbital rim back along the top of the zygomatic arch. The nerve runs through temporalis, so inject both deep and superficial to the temporalis fascia: the hardest nerve to block.
Auriculotemporal: 1 cm in front of and 1 cm above the tragus, feel the superficial temporal artery and inject just behind it. Stay above the tragus: the facial nerve is close below.
Great auricular (optional): usually covered by the lesser occipital injection, 1.5–2 cm behind the ear at the level of the tragus.
Lesser occipital: infiltrate behind the ear from the top of the ear to the lobule, then back along the superior nuchal line.
Greater occipital: feel the occipital artery about two-thirds of the way from the mastoid to the external occipital protuberance, on the superior nuchal line, and inject just medial to it.
Needle approach

Aspirate before each injection: the scalp is very vascular. Press on each site for a minute afterwards to spread the local anaesthetic and stop bruising.

Target and deposition

Each nerve where it becomes subcutaneous. The alternative is a ring block: infiltrate all the way round the head above a line from the occipital protuberance to the eyebrows, along the top of the ears. That takes about 30 ml.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

2–5 ml per site; 20–30 ml in total for one or both sides

With adrenaline 1:200 000. Absorption from the scalp is fast, so add up the total for both sides and any surgical infiltration.

Local anaesthetic toxicity: Keep the total dose within the maximum for the patient’s weight, especially with bilateral blocks or when combining blocks.

Coverage

Front

Right side

Back

Dense: reliable
Moderate: usually adequate
Variable: patchy, not reliable
One side shown (the patient’s right). Areas are schematic: nerve territories vary and overlap.
Supraorbital (V1): forehead and scalp back to the vertex
Supratrochlear (V1): the middle of the forehead
Auriculotemporal (V3): the temple and the front of the ear
Greater occipital (C2): the back of the scalp up to the vertex
Lesser occipital (C2): the scalp behind and above the ear
Zygomaticotemporal (V2): a small patch of temple beside the eyebrow
Great auricular (C2–C3): angle of the jaw, over the parotid, most of the ear

Covers: The scalp on one side: forehead to vertex (V1), temple (V2, V3) and the back of the head (C2).

MECHANISM

Every nerve to the scalp becomes superficial on a line around the head, so each can be reached with a few millilitres. The trigeminal branches supply the front and sides; the occipital nerves (C2–C3) the back.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Dense skin and pericranial analgesia when all sites are injected; enough for an awake craniotomy with sedation. The dura and brain are not covered: the surgeon infiltrates the dura near the middle meningeal artery if needed.

WHAT IT MISSES
The dura and temporalis muscle (deep), unless the zygomaticotemporal injection goes deep to the temporalis fascia.
The other side, for a midline or bifrontal incision.
Complications and how to avoid them
Bruising and haematoma are the commonest problems; press after each injection.
Intravascular injection and local anaesthetic toxicity: the scalp is very vascular; aspirate, use adrenaline, and keep within the maximum dose.
Facial nerve block (temporary facial weakness) from an auriculotemporal injection that is too low or deep.
A transient rise in heart rate and blood pressure from the adrenaline.
Practical pearls
The mnemonic GLASS Z: greater occipital, lesser occipital, auriculotemporal, supraorbital, supratrochlear and zygomaticotemporal.
Do the block before the pins go in: it blunts the haemodynamic response to pinning and incision.
For an awake craniotomy, ask the surgeon to infiltrate the pin sites and the incision as well.
Awake craniotomy

Used when the patient has to talk or move during the operation: tumours near the speech or motor cortex, epilepsy surgery and deep brain stimulation. The scalp block makes pinning, incision and the craniotomy bearable with light sedation, and gives analgesia afterwards.

Exam corner

PRACTICE QUESTION (VIVA)

Name the nerves you block for a scalp block, and where you find each one.

Model answer points
Front (trigeminal): supraorbital and supratrochlear (V1) at the orbital rim; zygomaticotemporal (V2) along the lateral orbital rim and zygomatic arch; auriculotemporal (V3) in front of the tragus behind the superficial temporal artery.
Back (C2–C3): greater occipital medial to the occipital artery on the superior nuchal line; lesser occipital behind the ear; great auricular optional.
Small volumes (2–5 ml) with adrenaline; aspirate; press; total about 20–30 ml.
Complications: haematoma, intravascular injection and toxicity, facial nerve block.

CHAPTER 3 OF 3 · SCALP · OCCIPITAL

Greater occipital nerve block

The greater occipital nerve (C2) supplies the back of the scalp up to the vertex. Block it on the superior nuchal line with landmarks, or more proximally at C2 with ultrasound, where it crosses obliquus capitis inferior.

USE IT FOR

Posterior craniotomy and VP shunt insertion or revision
Headache: occipital neuralgia, cervicogenic headache, migraine (pain clinic)
Part of a scalp block
POSITION
Sitting with the neck flexed, or prone or lateral
PROBE
Linear, along obliquus capitis inferior at C2 (ultrasound)
NEEDLE
25–27G (landmark) or 50 mm (ultrasound), in-plane, lateral to medial
DOSE
1–3 ml (landmark); 2–3 ml (ultrasound at C2)
COVERS
The back of the scalp, from the occipital protuberance to the vertex

Greater occipital nerve at C2: view along obliquus capitis inferior

Position

Sitting with the neck flexed and the forehead resting on a table, or prone, or lateral with the side to be blocked uppermost.

Equipment
25–27G needle for the landmark technique; a 50 mm needle and a linear probe for the ultrasound technique
1–3 ml of local anaesthetic per side.
Landmarks and scanning

Landmark (distal). The nerve lies about two-thirds of the way along a line from the mastoid to the external occipital protuberance, on the superior nuchal line, just medial to the occipital artery (easy to feel). Insert the needle at 90° to the occiput, aspirate and inject 1–3 ml; press on the site afterwards. Numbness over the top of the head shows success. The nerve’s position varies widely between people (1.5–7.5 cm from the midline), which is why blind blocks sometimes fail.

Ultrasound (proximal, at C2). Find the bifid C2 spinous process, then move laterally along obliquus capitis inferior. Here the nerve’s relation to the muscle is constant: it crosses the superficial surface of obliquus capitis inferior.

Needle approach

Ultrasound: in-plane, lateral to medial, to the plane between semispinalis capitis and obliquus capitis inferior.

Sonoanatomy

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Subcutaneous fat
Trapezius
Splenius capitis
Semispinalis capitis
Obliquus capitis inferior
Target and deposition

Distal: medial to the occipital artery at the superior nuchal line. Proximal: the nerve on top of obliquus capitis inferior, beneath semispinalis capitis.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

1–3 ml of local anaesthetic per side

Local anaesthetic toxicity: Keep the total dose within the maximum for the patient’s weight, especially with bilateral blocks or when combining blocks.

Coverage

Right side

Back

Dense: reliable
Variable: patchy, not reliable
One side shown (the patient’s right). Areas are schematic: nerve territories vary and overlap.
Greater occipital (C2): the back of the scalp up to the vertex
Lesser occipital (C2): the scalp behind and above the ear

Covers: The back of the scalp from the occipital protuberance to the vertex.

MECHANISM

The nerve leaves between C1 and C2, curves round obliquus capitis inferior, runs up through semispinalis capitis and trapezius, and becomes subcutaneous just below the superior nuchal line, medial to the occipital artery.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Dense in the nerve’s territory when the injection is right. The proximal (C2) ultrasound approach is more reliable because the nerve is in the same place in most people.

WHAT IT MISSES
Behind the ear: the lesser occipital nerve. Block it a third of the way along the same line from the mastoid, or infiltrate behind the ear.
The upper neck (C3 and below).
Complications and how to avoid them
Few, because the nerve is superficial. Intravascular injection (occipital artery): aspirate.
At C2: the vertebral artery lies deep to obliquus capitis inferior laterally, and the spinal cord deep and medially. Keep the tip superficial to the muscle.
Practical pearls
Feel for the occipital artery first: the nerve is just medial to it.
The lesser occipital nerve is a third of the way from the mastoid; the greater occipital two-thirds.
Exam corner

PRACTICE QUESTION (OSCE)

Describe how you would block the greater occipital nerve for a posterior fossa craniotomy.

Model answer points
Landmark: superior nuchal line, two-thirds from the mastoid to the occipital protuberance, medial to the occipital artery; 1–3 ml after aspiration; press.
Ultrasound at C2: bifid C2 spinous process, slide laterally along obliquus capitis inferior; nerve on the superficial surface of OCI; in-plane; 2–3 ml.
Add the lesser occipital nerve (a third of the way from the mastoid) for the area behind the ear.
Risks at C2: vertebral artery deep and lateral, spinal cord deep and medial.

STEP 1 OF 4 · SCAN

Start in the midline at the occiput and slide down: C1 has no spinous process, so the first bifid spinous process is C2. Then move the probe laterally and turn its lateral end up towards the mastoid, so it lies along obliquus capitis inferior.

STEP 2 OF 4 · IDENTIFY

From the skin down: trapezius (thin here), splenius capitis, semispinalis capitis, then obliquus capitis inferior running from C2 to C1. The greater occipital nerve is an oval between semispinalis capitis and obliquus capitis inferior. The vertebral artery is deep to OCI, laterally, near C1: check with colour Doppler.

STEP 3 OF 4 · NEEDLE

In-plane, lateral to medial, through the muscles to the plane between semispinalis capitis and obliquus capitis inferior, beside the nerve. Never go deep to OCI: the vertebral artery is lateral and deep, the spinal cord medial and deep.

STEP 4 OF 4 · INJECT

Aspirate, then inject 2–3 ml. The fluid opens the plane on top of OCI and surrounds the nerve.

Position

Sitting with the neck flexed and the forehead resting on a table, or prone, or lateral with the side to be blocked uppermost.

Equipment
25–27G needle for the landmark technique; a 50 mm needle and a linear probe for the ultrasound technique
1–3 ml of local anaesthetic per side.
Landmarks and scanning

Landmark (distal). The nerve lies about two-thirds of the way along a line from the mastoid to the external occipital protuberance, on the superior nuchal line, just medial to the occipital artery (easy to feel). Insert the needle at 90° to the occiput, aspirate and inject 1–3 ml; press on the site afterwards. Numbness over the top of the head shows success. The nerve’s position varies widely between people (1.5–7.5 cm from the midline), which is why blind blocks sometimes fail.

Ultrasound (proximal, at C2). Find the bifid C2 spinous process, then move laterally along obliquus capitis inferior. Here the nerve’s relation to the muscle is constant: it crosses the superficial surface of obliquus capitis inferior.

Needle approach

Ultrasound: in-plane, lateral to medial, to the plane between semispinalis capitis and obliquus capitis inferior.

Target and deposition

Distal: medial to the occipital artery at the superior nuchal line. Proximal: the nerve on top of obliquus capitis inferior, beneath semispinalis capitis.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

1–3 ml of local anaesthetic per side

Local anaesthetic toxicity: Keep the total dose within the maximum for the patient’s weight, especially with bilateral blocks or when combining blocks.

Coverage

Right side

Back

Dense: reliable
Variable: patchy, not reliable
One side shown (the patient’s right). Areas are schematic: nerve territories vary and overlap.
Greater occipital (C2): the back of the scalp up to the vertex
Lesser occipital (C2): the scalp behind and above the ear

Covers: The back of the scalp from the occipital protuberance to the vertex.

MECHANISM

The nerve leaves between C1 and C2, curves round obliquus capitis inferior, runs up through semispinalis capitis and trapezius, and becomes subcutaneous just below the superior nuchal line, medial to the occipital artery.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Dense in the nerve’s territory when the injection is right. The proximal (C2) ultrasound approach is more reliable because the nerve is in the same place in most people.

WHAT IT MISSES
Behind the ear: the lesser occipital nerve. Block it a third of the way along the same line from the mastoid, or infiltrate behind the ear.
The upper neck (C3 and below).
Complications and how to avoid them
Few, because the nerve is superficial. Intravascular injection (occipital artery): aspirate.
At C2: the vertebral artery lies deep to obliquus capitis inferior laterally, and the spinal cord deep and medially. Keep the tip superficial to the muscle.
Practical pearls
Feel for the occipital artery first: the nerve is just medial to it.
The lesser occipital nerve is a third of the way from the mastoid; the greater occipital two-thirds.
Exam corner

PRACTICE QUESTION (OSCE)

Describe how you would block the greater occipital nerve for a posterior fossa craniotomy.

Model answer points
Landmark: superior nuchal line, two-thirds from the mastoid to the occipital protuberance, medial to the occipital artery; 1–3 ml after aspiration; press.
Ultrasound at C2: bifid C2 spinous process, slide laterally along obliquus capitis inferior; nerve on the superficial surface of OCI; in-plane; 2–3 ml.
Add the lesser occipital nerve (a third of the way from the mastoid) for the area behind the ear.
Risks at C2: vertebral artery deep and lateral, spinal cord deep and medial.

us:
STEP 1 OF 4 · SCAN

Start in the midline at the occiput and slide down: C1 has no spinous process, so the first bifid spinous process is C2. Then move the probe laterally and turn its lateral end up towards the mastoid, so it lies along obliquus capitis inferior.

STEP 2 OF 4 · IDENTIFY

From the skin down: trapezius (thin here), splenius capitis, semispinalis capitis, then obliquus capitis inferior running from C2 to C1. The greater occipital nerve is an oval between semispinalis capitis and obliquus capitis inferior. The vertebral artery is deep to OCI, laterally, near C1: check with colour Doppler.

STEP 3 OF 4 · NEEDLE

In-plane, lateral to medial, through the muscles to the plane between semispinalis capitis and obliquus capitis inferior, beside the nerve. Never go deep to OCI: the vertebral artery is lateral and deep, the spinal cord medial and deep.

STEP 4 OF 4 · INJECT

Aspirate, then inject 2–3 ml. The fluid opens the plane on top of OCI and surrounds the nerve.
